title: Παῖς ⟨ἀκρίδας θηρεύων⟩ καὶ σκορπίος
titleEn: The Boy Hunting Locusts and the Scorpion
part: The Boy Hunting Locusts and the Scorpion (Chambry 293)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 293. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Παῖς πρὸ τοῦ τείχους ἀκρίδας ἐθήρευε.
sentences.tr: Pais pro tou teichous akridas ethēreue.
sentences.l: A boy in front of the wall was hunting locusts.
sentences.n: πρὸ τοῦ τείχους is the open ground outside the city wall, where a child could be let loose. ἐθήρευε is imperfect: the hunting is the standing situation the fable walks in upon.

sentences.t: Πολλὰς δὲ συλλαβών, ὡς ἐθεάσατο σκορπίον, οἰηθεὶς ἀκρίδα εἶναι, κοιλάνας τὴν χεῖρα, οἷός τε ἦν καταφέρειν αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Pollas de syllabōn, hōs etheasato skorpion, oiētheis akrida einai, koilanas tēn cheira, hoios te ēn katapherein auton.
sentences.l: And having caught many, when he saw a scorpion, thinking it to be a locust, and hollowing his hand, he was ready to bring the creature down.
sentences.i: He had taken a good many when he caught sight of a scorpion, and supposing it a locust he cupped his hand and was on the point of sweeping it in.
sentences.n: Three aorist participles in a row — συλλαβών, οἰηθείς, κοιλάνας — with one main verb at the end: the ordinary engine of these fables, best read as a chain of steps. οἷός τε ἦν, literally 'he was such as', is the idiom for being able or ready to do a thing. καταφέρω is 'bring down'; its object here is the scorpion, and the picture is of the hollowed hand sweeping the creature down into itself.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς τὸ κέντρον ἐπάρας εἶπεν· « Εἴθε γὰρ τοῦτο ἐποίησας, ἵνα καὶ ἃς συνείληφας ἀκρίδας ἀπολέσῃς. »
sentences.tr: Kai hos to kentron eparas eipen· « Eithe gar touto epoiēsas, hina kai has syneilēphas akridas apolesēis. »
sentences.l: And he, raising his sting, said: « Would that you had done this, so that you might lose the locusts you have caught as well. »
sentences.n: καὶ ὅς, 'and he', keeps the old demonstrative use of the relative pronoun — a fossil of earlier Greek, standard in narrative at a change of speaker. εἴθε with the aorist indicative is the wish for what did not happen; the scorpion's is bitter, since the blow would have cost the boy his catch along with more besides. In ἃς συνείληφας ἀκρίδας the noun has been drawn inside the relative clause: 'the locusts which you have caught'.

sentences.t: Οὗτος ὁ λόγος διδάσκει μὴ δεῖν πᾶσι τοῖς χρηστοῖς καὶ τοῖς πονηροῖς κατὰ ταὐτὰ προσφέρεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Houtos ho logos didaskei mē dein pasi tois chrēstois kai tois ponērois kata tauta prospheresthai.
sentences.l: This story teaches that one must not deal in the same way with all, the good and the wicked alike.
sentences.n: διδάσκει takes the infinitive of what is taught, here the impersonal μὴ δεῖν, 'that one must not'. ταὐτά is the crasis of τὰ αὐτά, and κατὰ ταὐτά is 'in the same way'. προσφέρομαι in the middle takes the dative of the person one deals with.
